name: Boxy leather reefer jacket

image.caption: Victorian Fashion of 1891 - Deutsch Catalogue Reefer Jackets and Hats Page 9

lead: A boxy leather reefer jacket takes the double-breasted, wide-lapelled shape of the naval reefer or pea coat and makes it in leather with a short, squared cut. People wear it to add structure across the shoulders and to keep the jacket's hem near the waist, which affects how the torso and legs appear in proportion.
The silhouette comes from naval outerwear; leather versions are a fashion adaptation. Little formal research addresses this specific garment.

paras: It is worn as an outer layer over a tee, knit or shirt. Fashion advice generally pairs a cropped hem with higher-rise trousers so that the length of the legs is emphasised.
Fit matters: a boxy cut can add bulk on narrow or very short frames, and genuine leather needs periodic conditioning. There are no medical risks.

angle.text: The jacket's structure and cropped hem change how the torso is outlined. How much it flatters depends on the wearer's frame and fit.

lead: A boxy leather reefer jacket is a cropped, squared-off, double-breasted leather jacket based on the naval reefer jacket. Wearers use it to build a structured upper-body outline and a short hem that keeps visual attention at the waist.

A reefer jacket is traditionally the officer's or chief petty officer's version of the pea coat, with the same double-breasted design but gold buttons and epaulettes; a longer variant is called a bridge coat.[1][2] The pea coat itself is a short, heavy coat first worn by European sailors and later American navies, and has been issued by the US Navy since 1897.[2]
No published studies address the leather boxy version specifically.

paras: Pea coats are short, with broad lapels, a double-breasted front and often three or four large buttons in two rows; reefer jackets share that design, with gold buttons and epaulettes in naval versions.[1][2] The boxy leather adaptation keeps the double-breasted front but cuts the body square and short.

The pea coat has been recorded in American newspapers as a 'pea-jacket' since the 1720s, and the US Navy has issued a standard version since 1897.[2] Moving the design to leather is a later fashion adaptation; the pea coat references loaded do not discuss leather versions.

timeline.event: US Navy begins issuing its standard pea coat.[2]
